cards.back: Create the identity with proper rights, then disable the account, revoke sessions and tokens, and transfer asset ownership when no longer needed.
Verifying that the real person matches the claimed identity before issuing credentials. MFA does not protect against a fake identity.
User, privileged global, privileged local, service, third-party, emergency access.
Service = automated task, dedicated and least privilege; emergency = break-glass access locked day-to-day with a logged procedure.
Trust between distinct domains: an identity provider authenticates and the service accepts the assertion without creating a local account.
Single Sign-On: one authentication for multiple applications. Convenient, but centralizes risk if the identity account is compromised.
Lightweight Directory Access Protocol: querying a directory of accounts, groups, and attributes. It is not a federation protocol.
Signed assertions exchanged between IdP and service provider: federated authentication.
Delegating authorization to a third-party app with limited scopes, without sharing the password. Authorization ≠ authentication.
Something you know (password, PIN), something you have (token, OTP), something you are (biometrics). Two factors from the same category are not MFA.
Dedicated hardware token; software token in an app; one-time password (TOTP/HOTP).
Biometrics = "something you are" factor, irrevocable data; backup code = single-use recovery factor, stored offline.
Role-Based Access Control: permissions attached to a role, inherited by users. Easy to audit and revoke.
Explicit rules applied to all (ACL, IP range); allowed time window (hours, expiration).
Discretionary Access Control: the resource owner decides who has access. Flexible, but permission sprawl is hard to track.
Mandatory Access Control: security labels and central policy enforce the decision, even against the owner.
Just-in-time access: elevated privilege granted for a short duration, often approved, with automatic revocation.
Periodic review by the resource owner: every permission must remain justified and revocations must be logged.
Passkey = phishing-resistant cryptographic credential; passwordless = authentication without a memorized secret.
Outdated recommendation: length, breach-checking, and MFA take priority per NIST SP 800-63B.
